content.text: I want to think about how we might use something like needle 3 from cactus compute. https://cactuscompute.com/needle. Currently we might have context sensitive buttons that popup for different features inside the application, say for some of the research that exists we could use it to help do intelligent search if we combine it with some document source that we provided as well. This can help with grounding what we are searching for when it is local. We can also have needle act as a little embedding system for us to intelligently do a lot of stuff. if we say had a bunch of documents that we downloaded locally and we were writing a legal document or report that could seriously help things. We could also relate to other written pieces that you have. Needle can also do classification style tasks and extraction tasks, extraction might be useful along with tool calling in automatically doing searches for things. It isn't going to do as well with things that require tacit knowledge but it is extremely cheap. Then we can use some thing like a reranker to test how relevant the different options are. The great thing is that we can use needle to do a lot of the smaller tasks, intelligent hooks, and we want to think of adding intelligence to the application in as many ways as possible to assist the user quickly.
I'll start by understanding what Needle 3 actually is, and in parallel explore how research/search currently works in Twyne.

# Needle 3 — Overview

**What it is:** A foundation model from Cactus aimed at automation on very small hardware — phones, wearables, robots, smart home, automotive, and microcontrollers.

## Size / parameters
- Shipped as a single binary in the "8-29 MB" range (the model page also mentions "9 to 29 MB CQ2-bit binaries" for the laddered subnetworks).
- Parameter count spans "29-121M Laddered Simple Attention Networks, CQ2 quantisation" — roughly 29M at the smallest usable depth up to 121M at full depth, of which ~70.8M sit in engram tables.
- Uses "Intelligence laddering": every layer is a usable sub-network, selectable from 2 layers up to 20. Four layers ≈ 8 MB, all twenty ≈ 29 MB.
- Vocabulary is a SentencePiece BPE tokenizer with 8,192 pieces; embedding is 8,192 × 768 with tied unembedding.
- Trained on "360B tokens of proprietary structured dataset".

## Supported tasks
- **Tool calling** — selects functions and fills arguments; supports multiple ordered calls, and returns an empty list rather than fabricating a call when nothing fits.
- **Structured extraction** — you declare a schema, it returns typed fields; a decode grammar ensures the output is parseable. Cactus says this "generalised well to classification problems too."
- **Text embeddings** — the same model emits sentence vectors for local search, tool matching, and de-duplicating alerts.
- **Reranking is not mentioned** anywhere in the page.

## Context length
Not stated explicitly. The only related detail is architectural: attention uses a "window 1024" with global attention at layers 4, 9, 14, and 19.

## Deployment
On-device across a wide target list, each shipping "a prebuilt engine under 1 MB" that loads `needle3.cact` weights:
- macOS (arm64), Linux (x86_64, arm64, armv7, riscv64, mipsel), Windows (x86_64, arm64)
- Android (arm64, armv7, riscv64), iOS (arm64, sim-arm64), tvOS, watchOS
- Browser via WASM (`needle.js`, `needle.wasm`) and a WASI component

Most targets ship a CLI plus `libneedle.a` and `needle.h`; Apple mobile/TV/watch targets ship the static library and header only. Distribution is a **Python package** — no npm package or native mobile SDK is described. The inference engine is downloaded once from Hugging Face and cached.

## Licensing / pricing
Not covered on the page. Source lives on GitHub (cactus-compute/needle); a **Cactus Platform** is offered for datasets, 2-bit quantisation, evaluation, and full-depth fine-tuning, but no prices or license terms appear.

## Performance
- Raspberry Pi 5: "400-4k tokens/s decode and 1-10k tokens/s prefill".
- Architecture claim: "spends over 2x fewer MFLOPs per token than a transformer of the same configuration."
- Accuracy positioning: it aims to "beat models 10x its size" on mobile tool calls and match 2–3x larger models on extraction.
- Fine-tuning on DroidCall reportedly "lifts every subnetwork by 18 to 36 points," with tuned subnetworks from 4 layers up surpassing DeepSeek V4 Flash, "starting at 29M parameters."
- Sample response fields include `prefill_tps` 4300.0, `decode_tps` 850.0, `peak_ram_mb` 28.5.

## API / SDK details
- Define tools by decorating a function; the type signature supplies argument types and the docstring becomes the description. `run()` closes the loop — model picks the call, Needle runs your function, feeds the result back, and attaches executed results under `results`.
- `triggers` accepts regexes; a match narrows decoding to those tools and forces a call, even under the confidence floor.
- `extract()` takes text plus a Pydantic model and returns a typed object.
- Each turn yields one JSON object with fields such as `type`, `success`, `error`, `function_calls`, `reasoning`, `confidence`, and the throughput/RAM stats above.
- **Confidence gating:** a calibrated head produces a score; the engine enforces a floor of 0.1, and anything below lands in `suppressed_calls` with `function_calls` left empty. Higher scores are yours to route on.
- **Fine-tuning CLI:** `needle finetune...

Based on the README content above, here's what I can and can't confirm:

**(1) JavaScript/TypeScript/npm/WASM binding** — Not documented. The only package shown is Python: `pip install cactus-needle`, called via `import needle`. There is a passing mention that the devices guide covers "the browser, WASI" and a "C API," but no npm package name or JS call signature appears on this page.

**(2) Embeddings** — Supported as a capability, but no API is shown. The README says the model returns "a vector for a sentence, so an app can search, match and route locally." No embedding dimension is stated anywhere in this content.

**(3) Classification and extraction** — Yes, both. Structured extraction works by declaring a shape and passing in unstructured text to get typed fields back; the README notes "The decode grammar guarantees the output parses, and extraction generalises to classification." The only concrete API shown is the tool-calling pattern: decorate a function with `@needle.tool`, construct `needle.Needle(tools=[...])`, and call `agent.run(...)`. Each turn returns a single JSON object containing `function_calls`, `reasoning`, and `confidence`. A linked guide describes extraction as using "the record as the only tool" with "classification with enums," but that guide's contents aren't in this page.

**(4) License** — Apache-2.0.

**(5) Model files, sizes, weights** — The weights file is `needle3.cact`, referenced in commands like `needle build --platform macos-arm64` and `./macos-arm64/needle --model needle3.cact --tools tools.json --serve`. The whole model is described as "a single 8-29 MB binary," with the largest at 121M parameters and fine-tuned subnetworks "starting at 29M parameters." Weights and platform engines are hosted on Hugging Face at `Cactus-Compute/needle3`. Each deployment target ships "a prebuilt engine under 1 MB." The `.cact` format uses "Cactus Quants at 2.125 bits per weight." Local fine-tuning "trains and exports at 4 bits."

**(6) Browser / WebGPU / WASM / SIMD / threads** — Essentially undocumented here. There's a browser demo at cactuscompute.com/needle, and the devices guide is said to cover the browser and WASI, but this page states no WebGPU, WASM, SIMD, or threading requirements. Platform targets shown are `macos-arm64` and `linux-arm64`.

**One operational note worth flagging:** telemetry is on by default in the binary. To disable it, set `NEEDLE_TELEMETRY=0` and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`.

For the gaps — npm/JS bindings, embedding dimension and API, and browser requirements — you'd need the linked devices guide and Python docs, or the `llms.txt` file in the repo, which the README says carries the same reference material for AI coding assistants.

Reading the Needle 3 API reference now — a few important constraints already surfaced. Still waiting on the two codebase explorers.

Key things I've pinned down so far:

- **There is no official JS/npm SDK.** Distribution is a Python package. There *is* a `wasm` and `wasm-component` (WASI Preview 2) platform build you can `needle download`, plus a sub-1MB C engine + `needle3.cact` weights (~35MB), but you'd be driving the WASM yourself or leaning on a third-party wrapper (`@supercmdk/needle` exists on npm, published by an individual).
- **Embeddings are not a public API.** The page markets "text embeddings," but the actual reference only exposes embeddings internally, as a tool-retrieval head that picks the top-5 tools when you declare more than five (`tool_index_path` persists that index). There's no `embed()` call and no stated dimension. So the "Needle as our embedding system for a local document corpus" idea doesn't have an API behind it today.
- **No reranker**, confirmed — nothing in the reference.
- **No free text, ever.** `type: "call"` or `"respond"`, and "the answer is the tool results, no free text is generated." Off-topic input returns an empty `function_calls` list. This is a router/extractor, not a small chat model.
- What it *does* give you is genuinely good for hooks: a byte-level grammar that guarantees well-formed calls, a **calibrated confidence score** in [0,1] with auto-suppression below 0.1, regex `triggers` that force-route a phrasing to a tool, and `extract(text, schema)` which doubles as classification via enums. Plus LoRA fine-tuning to a 4-bit `.cact`.

That last cluster — confidence gating and triggers — maps well onto your "context-sensitive buttons that pop up" idea: confidence is exactly the signal for *show the button vs. act vs. stay quiet*.

# Twyne research / "Apparatus" subsystem

## 1. The research provider abstraction

There are **two distinct provider layers**, and the naming is a bit subtle:

### Layer A — `ApparatusResearchProvider`: *which route the search takes*

Defined in `/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/src/types/index.ts:917`:

```ts
export type ApparatusResearchProvider =
  | "hosted"
  | "search-api"
  | "model-web-search"
  | "web-mcp";
```

with the doc comment:

> `hosted:` Twyne's own service, using the server's provider key. `search-api:` a search API called straight from this browser (BYOK), configured by `searchBackend`. `model-web-search:` the writer's own model provider, with web search on. `web-mcp:` tools discovered from the writer's MCP servers.

Stored in `ApparatusSettings` (`src/types/index.ts:~995`):

```ts
export interface ApparatusSettings {
  defaultCitationStyle: ApparatusCitationStyle;
  aiEnhanceCitations: boolean;
  flagMissingSources: boolean;
  autoInsertFootnotes: boolean;
  researchProvider: ApparatusResearchProvider;
  searchBackend: SearchBackendConfig;
  maxResults: number;              // sources requested per claim
  mcpServers: McpServerConfig[];
}
```

Default is `researchProvider: "hosted"`, `maxResults: 8`.

### Layer B — `SearchBackendAdapter`: *which vendor answers a BYOK search*

`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/src/utils/research-backends.ts` — this is the clean pluggable interface:

```ts
export interface SearchRequest {
  query: string;
  context: string;
  maxResults: number;
}

export interface SearchBackendAdapter {
  id: SearchBackendId;
  label: string;
  /** Shown in settings so the writer knows where to get a key. */
  keyHint: string;
  defaultUrl: string;
  /** Whether the writer must supply their own endpoint. */
  requiresUrl?: boolean;
  buildRequest(req: SearchRequest, config: SearchBackendConfig): { url: string; init: RequestInit };
  /** Pull the result array out of the parsed response body. */
  extract(body: unknown, config: SearchBackendConfig): unknown;
}
```

`SearchBackendId = "tinyfish" | "exa" | "tavily" | "brave" | "serper" | "custom"` (`src/types/index.ts:~926`). **TinyFish is the default** (`DEFAULT_SEARCH_BACKEND = { id: "tinyfish", apiKey: "", baseUrl: "", resultsPath: "" }`), endpoint `https://api.search.tinyfish.ai/v1/search`. `searchBackend(id)` falls back to `SEARCH_BACKENDS.tinyfish` for unknown ids.

Adding a vendor is one entry in `SEARCH_BACKENDS`. `toSource()` / `toSources()` normalize any vendor shape into `Source` by reading every common field spelling (`title|name|heading`, `snippet|description|text|content|summary|excerpt`, etc.), require an `http(s)` URL, dedupe by URL, truncate snippets at 1200 chars. `runSearchBackend()` is the entry point.

### The hosted path (server-side)

`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/convex/research.ts` (`"use node"`). Header states the whole contract:

```
searchSources({ query, context }) -> { results: Source[] }
fetchSource  ({ url })            -> { title, author, …, markdown, embeddable }
```

Canonical types:

```ts
export interface Source {
  title: string;
  url: string;
  snippet: string;
  author?: string;
  publisher?: string;
  date?: string;
  why?: string;
}

export interface FetchedSource {
  title: string;
  author?: string;
  publisher?: string;
  date?: string;
  markdown: string;
  embeddable: boolean;
}
```

A server-side `ProviderSpec` table mirrors the client adapters (`tinyfish | exa | tavily | brave | serper | custom`), selected by env: `RESEARCH_PROVIDER` (default `"tinyfish"`), `RESEARCH_API_KEY` (falls back to `TINYFISH_API_KEY`), `RESEARCH_SEARCH_URL`, `RESEARCH_FETCH_URL`. TinyFish is the only provider with a distinct fetch endpoint baked in (`https://api.fetch.tinyfish.ai/v1/fetch`, `format: "markdown"`).

Both actions are rate-limited (`consumeRateLimit` with `RATE_LIMITS.research` for Pro, `RATE_LIMITS.researchFree` otherwise) and return `provider: "local"` with a deterministic stub when signed out or unkeyed. The client explicitly **rejects** the local stub as evidence (`background-research.ts:~685`): *"local placeholder results are not fact-check evidence."*

Note: `fetchSource` is defined but has **no caller in `src/`** — only `searchSources` is invoked (`background-research.ts:681`). The apparatus route has `embedUrl/embedMarkdown/embedProvider` store fields, so the URL→markdown reader is wired in the UI store but the action call isn't reachable from the search I ran; worth a closer look if you need it.

## 3. Embeddings / vector search / semantic search

**None. There is no embedding, vector, or semantic-search code in this repo.**

- `convex/schema.ts` uses only `.index(...)` — no `.vectorIndex(...)`, no `.searchIndex(...)`. The only `vectorIndex` / `ctx.vectorSearch` hits anywhere are in the vendored doc `convex/_generated/ai/guidelines.md:282-293` (Convex's own docs, not app code).
- No `cosine`, `similarity` (as a function), `tf-idf`, `bm25`, `jaccard` implementations. `research-targets.ts:137,168` mentions "topical similarity" only as prompt text telling the model that topical similarity is *not* enough.
- The only "embedding"-adjacent artifacts are **voice embeddings** for the TTS model (`voices/F1.bin` etc. in `browser-inference.ts`) and the phrase "embedding it in a regular expression" in `find-replace.ts:35`.
- Ranking is purely heuristic — `rankSourcesForTarget` in `src/utils/research-targets.ts:373`:

```ts
score:
  (source.snippet && source.snippet.trim().length >= 40 ? 1 : 0) +
  (source.author ? 0.5 : 0) +
  (source.publisher ? 0.5 : 0) +
  (source.title ? 0.25 : 0) +
  Math.max(0, 1 - index * 0.2);   // provider order as a weak prior
```

So a RAG/vector layer would be entirely greenfield.

5	# Confidence
6	
7	> How TypeSafe reports certainty, how it differs from probability, and how to use it to control system behavior.
8	
9	All Score and Choice answers from TypeSafe include a `probabilities` property representing the probability distribution across the options (for Choice) or levels (for Score). The *shape* of that distribution is what tells you how certain the model is: concentrated on one outcome means a confident answer, spread out means an uncertain one.
10	
11	The answer's `confidence` property collapses that shape into a single number from 0 to 1, so you can threshold on it without doing the math yourself. (Noul answers don't carry one.)
12	
13	## Confidence is derived from the probabilities
14	
15	`confidence` is a statistic computed from the probability distribution the answer already gives you. TypeSafe computes it for you and returns it on every Choice and Score answer, so the common case needs no extra work on your side.
16	
17	<Note>
18	  **A solid default:** We provide `confidence` as a convenient measure that fits most use-cases, but you are never locked into our definition. Depending on what you are evaluating, a different measure may serve you better, which is exactly why we give you the full `probabilities` in the response. The pros and cons of different computations is a specialized topic that we'll keep to a separate cookbook rather than this page, and will add the link here when we do!
19	</Note>
20	
21	For a [Choice](/primitives/choice), the distribution is `probabilities` across your options. For a [Score](/primitives/score), it is the distribution across your levels. In both cases a flatter distribution means lower confidence: low confidence on a Choice often means none of the options are a clear winner over the others, and low confidence on a Score often means the levels are ambiguous, multi-dimensional, or the state doesn't contain enough to go on.
22	
23	## "I don't know" is a useful signal
24	
25	If an intelligent system, whether human or machine, cannot express honest uncertainty, the system cannot be trusted.
26	
27	Confidence gives you a built-in mechanism for the model to say "I'm not sure about this one." This lets your code implement different behavior for different levels of certainty, which is the foundation for building systems you can actually rely on.
28	
29	## Three paths for using confidence in your code
30	
31	A useful starting pattern is to divide confidence into three ranges, each producing a different system behavior:
32	
33	**High confidence:** Act automatically. The model has a clear read and you can proceed without human involvement.
34	
35	**Medium confidence:** Proceed with caution. The model has a reasonable answer but is not certain. Depending on context, you might ask the user to confirm, flag for review, or gather more information before acting.
36	
37	**Low confidence:** Do not act. Route to a human, request clarification, or fall back to a different system. The model is telling you it does not have enough information or the question is not a good fit.
38	
39	Where you draw those boundaries depends on the stakes.
40	
41	## Thresholds scale with risk
42	
43	A confidence threshold is not one number. Different actions within the same system should be gated at different levels depending on the consequences of getting it wrong.

|---|---|---|

# Browser models

What ships in the model selector, what is queued behind it, and what has already
been ruled out. Every size below was measured from the Hugging Face blob API
(sum of the chosen dtype's `.onnx` plus its `.onnx_data*` chunks, plus tokenizer
and config files) — not read off a model card.

The registry lives in `web/src/stores/local-model.ts`. Read this file before
adding to it: most of the obvious candidates are already here with a reason.

## What a model needs to run here

Four things have to be true. Each has cost us a model.

1. **An ONNX export in the transformers.js layout.** `onnx/model_q4f16.onnx`
   for text models, or the four-way `embed_tokens` / `decoder_model_merged` /
   `vision_encoder` / `audio_encoder` split for multimodal Gemma. GGUF, MLX,
   safetensors, and onnxruntime-genai layouts are all unloadable — the loader
   fetches paths that do not exist and fails as a 404.
2. **Weights quantized to 4-bit or 8-bit.** ONNX Runtime's `MatMulNBits` kernel
   accepts nothing else; sub-4-bit weights fail at session creation with
   `bits must be 4 or 8`. That string lives in the ORT WASM binary, so no
   loader-side dtype config works around it. Ternary and q2 exports are out
   until onnxruntime-web adds support.
3. **An architecture transformers.js implements.** `lfm2`, `lfm2_moe`,
   `lfm2_vl`, `qwen3`, and the Gemma families are in; a `trust_remote_code`
   architecture with custom modeling files is not.
4. **A download and a VRAM footprint a browser can carry.** Roughly: the
   download is also what has to fit on the GPU.

Multi-part external data (`model_q4f16.onnx_data_1`, `_2`, …) is fine as long as
the repo declares chunk counts in `transformers.js_config.use_external_data_format`.
Both shipped exports do.

- In Convex 1.41+, `ctx.runQuery` and `ctx.runMutation` accept an optional third argument with `transactionLimits`. These limits cap how much the nested call may additionally consume on top of what the caller has already used - they can only tighten the global transaction limits, never raise them. If the nested call exceeds its cap and rolls back, the caller keeps its own remaining budget, which is useful for preserving caller headroom. For example:

-### 11. Feature flags
+### 11. Persona-note quality gate — `src/utils/note-gate.ts` ✅ BUILT
+Jev grades every persona note before the writer sees it, on three Score dimensions
+(`helpful`, `actionable`, `servesGoal`) plus two Nouls against the brief
+(`violatesConstraints`, `movesSuccessSignal`). Below threshold, the note is **sent back to
+the frontier model to rewrite**, carrying the Jev verdict as the instruction.
+
+- **This inverts the ladder**: the cheap engine gates the expensive one, rather than backing
+  it up. Jev costs ~$0.00006 per note; a persona rewrite costs a frontier call, so the gate
+  pays for itself the first time it suppresses a useless note.
+- **Quality averages; constraints veto.** Averaging them together would let a high
+  `helpful` score buy off a constraint the writer declared non-negotiable — exactly
+  backwards. `maxViolationRisk` defaults to **0.75, not 0.5**, because a Noul at 0.5 means
+  *genuinely uncertain*, and discarding advice on a coin flip throws away good notes.
+- **The rewrite instruction quotes the level description, not the number.** "Vague —
+  gestures at a problem without locating it" tells a model what to fix; `helpful: 2.1`
+  does not.
+- `MAX_REWRITES = 2`, and `bestAttempt()` keeps the **best** attempt rather than the last;
+  an un-vetoed attempt always beats a vetoed one regardless of score.
+- Only constraints that `brief-coach.enforceableConstraints()` classifies as `hard` or
+  `editorial` may trigger the veto — which closes the loop where an *uncheckable*
+  constraint would otherwise make the veto fire at random.
+
+### 12. Passage triage — `src/utils/passage-triage.ts` ✅ BUILT
+Jev reads the draft and decides **what needs attention and what to leave alone**, so the
+room fans out to the passages that earn it instead of the whole manuscript.
+
+- Five labels that map onto surfaces Twyne already has — `nothing` / `advice` / `question`
+  / `evidence` / `cut`. A label with nowhere to go is a label that produces noise.
+- **Criticality is a separate question from need.** A broken throwaway line and a subtly
+  weak thesis both come back as "advice"; only the second is worth a frontier call, and
+  nothing but `priority = need × criticality` distinguishes them.
+- **Needle offline path**: `TRIAGE_ENUM` is the same closed label set for Needle's
+  `extract()`. Offline results carry `confidence: null` and `criticality: null` honestly —
+  ranking collapses, because without a criticality signal there is no ranking to make, and
+  a made-up number in front of the writer is worse than none.
+
+### 13. Brief coach — `src/utils/brief-coach.ts` ✅ BUILT
+Jev grades each of the seven interview fields for sufficiency, asks whether the brief as a
+whole is enough to write from, and interrogates each stated constraint: **"is this a real
+non-negotiable?"**
+
+- Constraints classify as `hard` / `editorial` / `preference` / `uncheckable`. The split is
+  mechanical, not pedantic: a **preference** recorded as a constraint will silently suppress
+  good advice, and an **uncheckable** one will make the note-gate veto fire at random.
+- **Jev cannot generate text.** It cannot write "your audience is too broad — who
+  specifically?". Every hint in this module is therefore an authored constant *selected* by
+  a classification. Designing past that limit would have produced a module that silently
+  returns nothing.
+- `briefIsLoadBearing()` guards the rest of the ladder: when the brief is vague, `targetFit`
+  is measuring the brief rather than the draft, and a confident-looking score is a lie.
+

+/**
+ * System One (Jev) judgements, routed through Not Organic.
+ *
+ * Jev is hosted and needs a credential, so it cannot be called from the
+ * browser. The credential belongs to **Not Organic**, not to this deployment:
+ * Not Organic is the account/control plane, so it owns provider keys, per
+ * customer metering, and entitlement — exactly as it already does for chat,
+ * embeddings, images, audio and Tavus. Twyne holds no TypeSafe key in
+ * production; it presents a DPoP-bound product assertion and calls
+ * `POST /v1/judgement`, the same shape `providerIdentity.ts` uses for
+ * `/v1/wallet` and `/v1/billing/checkout`.
+ *
+ * That boundary is what makes the tier reusable: every other property gets
+ * judgements from one place, one key rotates in one place, and spend is
+ * attributable per account rather than per deployment.
+ *
+ * `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` survives as a **local-development fallback only**, for
+ * working on a judgement surface without the gateway running. It is never the
+ * production path; if Not Organic is enabled the direct key is ignored.
+ *
+ * The question/answer shapes live in `src/utils/system-one.ts`, which is
+ * transport-free and shared with the client. Deliberately no `"use node"`:
+ * `fetch()` and WebCrypto both work in the default Convex runtime, and the
+ * lighter runtime starts faster for what is a ~380 ms call.
+ */
+

+ * to a concrete Jev version, the same indirection as the `fast`/`balanced`
+ * aliases — so a Jev upgrade is a gateway deploy, not a release in every
+ * product that asks questions.

+const JUDGEMENT_PATH = "/v1/judgement";

+

*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /tmp/notorganic-judgement/INSTALL.md
+# `/v1/judgement` — Jev as a provider capability
+
+Adds System One (TypeSafe Jev) to the Not Organic gateway as a first-class
+route, so every property gets typed judgements from one place, one credential
+rotates in one place, and spend is attributable per account.
+
+Modelled on the Tavus integration: a vendor-specific service module plus one
+`protectedRoute`. Four changes, one of them a new file.
+
+---
+
+## 1. New file — `apps/gateway/src/judgement.ts`
+
+Copy `judgement.ts` from this directory. It owns validation, the upstream
+call, and reserve → settle metering against `config.store`.
+
+## 2. `apps/gateway/src/types.ts` — add the config block
+
+Inside `interface GatewayConfig`, beside the existing `tavus?` block:
+
+```ts
+  /** Provider-owned TypeSafe credentials. No field here is returned to products. */
+  typesafe?: {
+    apiKey: string;
+    /** Concrete Jev version the `judgement` alias resolves to. */
+    model?: string;
+    apiOrigin?: string;
+  };
+```
+
+## 3. `apps/gateway/src/main.ts` — read the env
+
+Beside the existing `tavus` block (~line 219):
+
+```ts
+let typesafe: GatewayConfig["typesafe"];
+if (Bun.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY?.trim()) {
+  typesafe = {
+    apiKey: required("TYPESAFE_API_KEY"),
+    ...(Bun.env.TYPESAFE_MODEL?.trim()
+      ? { model: Bun.env.TYPESAFE_MODEL.trim() }
+      : {}),
+  };
+}
+```
+
+and add `typesafe,` to the `const config: GatewayConfig = { ... }` literal,
+beside `tavus,`.
+
+## 4. `apps/gateway/src/app.ts` — register the route
+
+Import beside the Tavus import (~line 20):
+
+```ts
+import { JudgementGateway } from "./judgement";
+```
+
+Instantiate beside `const tavus = new TavusGateway(config);` (~line 168):
+
+```ts
+  const judgement = new JudgementGateway(config);
+```
+
+Register beside the Tavus routes (~line 574). `judgement:evaluate` is the
+capability Twyne already requests in its product assertion:
+
+```ts
+  protectedRoute(
+    app,
+    tokens,
+    "post",
+    "/v1/judgement",
+    "judgement:evaluate",
+    async (c) => {
+      const raw = await c.req.raw.clone().arrayBuffer();
+      const digest = await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", raw);
+      const requestHash = Buffer.from(new Uint8Array(digest)).toString(
+        "base64url",
+      );
+      // Products that omit the header get content-addressed idempotency
+      // rather than a 400 — a judgement is safe to deduplicate by body.
+      const idempotencyKey =
+        c.req.header("idempotency-key")?.slice(0, 255) || requestHash;
+      return c.json(
+        await judgement.evaluate(
+          c.get("principal"),
+          await c.req.json().catch(() => null),
+          idempotencyKey,
+          requestHash,
+        ),
+      );
+    },
+  );
+```
+
+### Optional: advertise it in `/v1/models`
+
+`judgement` is a logical model, so products can discover it. In the
+`/v1/models` fallback list (~line 543) add `"judgement"`. Note the existing
+comment there — only advertise it on deployments where `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` is
+actually set, otherwise it promises a tier that 503s when called.
+
+---
+
+## Deployment
+
+Set on the **gateway** service only:
+
+```
+TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<from `skate get typesafe_api_key@secrets`>
+TYPESAFE_MODEL=jev-latest        # optional
+```
+
+Then remove `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from any product deployment. Twyne prefers Not
+Organic whenever `NOTORGANIC_ENABLED` is set and ignores a local key in that
+case, so the two can overlap safely during the cutover.
+
+## Pricing note
+
+$0.042 per million input tokens, output free, which is exactly **0.042
+microUSD per input token** — the constant in `judgement.ts`. A full
+11-criterion rubric pass measured 1,401 input tokens ≈ 59 microUSD, about
+17,000 passes per dollar. Reservation is a chars/4 estimate with a 2× safety
+factor; settlement uses the real `usage.input_tokens` TypeSafe returns.
+
+## Verifying
+
+```sh
+curl -sS https://api.notorganic.info/v1/judgement \
+  -H "authorization: DPoP <token>" -H "dpop: <proof>" \
+  -H "content-type: application/json" -H "idempotency-key: $(uuidgen)" \
+  -d '{"state":{"draft":"Remote work is obviously the future."},
+       "questions":{"integrity":{"type":"score",
+         "instructions":"Rate unsupported certainty.",
+         "criteria":["Poor","Weak","Adequate","Strong","Excellent"]}}}'
+```
+
+Expect `{ model, answers: { integrity: { type: "score", score, legend,
+probabilities, confidence } }, usage }`, and a matching row in the account's
+usage ledger.
*** End Patch

content.text:
Wired, with one deliberate stop short of the finish line.

## The architecture you asked for

You're right that this belongs in Not Organic, and the codebase agreed more than I expected — `convex/lib/notorganic.ts` already had `providerJsonRequest()`, the exact helper a `/judgement` route needs, and `providerIdentity.ts` already calls `/v1/wallet` and `/v1/billing/checkout` that way. So this wasn't a new pattern, just an unused one.

**Twyne side** (`convex/systemOne.ts`) now prefers Not Organic and falls back to a direct key only for local dev:

```
notOrganicEnabled()  →  POST /v1/judgement   (DPoP product assertion, capability judgement:evaluate)
TYPESAFE_API_KEY     →  direct TypeSafe       (developer machines only)
neither              →  { ok: false, error: "unconfigured" }
```

One decision worth flagging: **Not Organic wins even when both are configured.** A machine with both is mid-migration, and silently preferring the local key there ships a surface never exercised against the real boundary.

**Provider side** — `apps/gateway/src/judgement.ts` is installed. Modelled on Tavus, because Jev has the same shape problem: it isn't chat, so forcing it through `/v1/chat/completions` would mean inventing a prompt envelope and parsing text back out — the exact round trip the model exists to remove.

Per-customer inspection works through the real ledger: `store.reserve` → `markDispatched` → `markAccepted` → `settle`, billed on Jev's actual `usage.input_tokens`. Pricing lands neatly — $0.042/Mtok input with free output is exactly **0.042 microUSD per input token**, so a full rubric pass is ~59 microUSD.

## What I stopped short of

The remaining three edits are to `types.ts`, `main.ts` and `app.ts` — **all three are already dirty in your provider repo**, along with `proxy.ts` and `auth.ts`. Interleaving with in-flight work there is how changes get tangled, so I staged exact snippets in `apps/gateway/src/judgement.INSTALL.md` instead. Say the word and I'll apply them.

Two bugs I caught in my own module by typechecking it in place:
- **Telemetry was leaking identity** — I passed properties where `distinctId` goes. `PortkeyProxy` keys analytics by an HMAC pseudonym of the account ID, never the raw ID. Fixed to match, with a TODO to export `pseudonym()` rather than keep my copy.
- A brace error that closed the class early.

Remaining errors are only the three `typesafe` config references — install step 2.

## Also wired

`runRubricPass()` in `rubric-grade.ts` — the missing seam joining pure grading to transport. Takes a caller, returns a `RubricGrade`, degrades rather than throws. **1104 tests pass, 0 fail**; typecheck and Prettier clean.

I did **not** refactor `rubric-panel.tsx`. It has six existing frontier-call paths across ~800 lines, and doing that safely in the same breath as an auth-boundary change would make both hard to review. It's now a one-function call away.

Next: apply the three gateway edits, set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` on the **gateway** service (not Twyne's Convex), then wire the panel.
